title: How do you answer "Tell me about a time you failed" without hurting your chances?
description: How to answer the failure question in consulting interviews honestly, with weak and strong example answers and the mistakes to avoid.
hook: You answer "Tell me about a time you failed" by choosing a real mistake that was clearly yours, stating its consequence plainly, and spending most of your answer on what you changed afterwards and the evidence that the change worked. The question makes people nervous, so many dodge it with a disguised strength. Interviewers spot that immediately and it costs trust. A real failure, told calmly, is far more convincing.
body:
What the interviewer is testing

Consultants make mistakes, and clients see some of them. The interviewer wants to know three things: will you own an error rather than hide it, can you see what caused it, and do you change your behaviour as a result? A candidate who talks about failure calmly and specifically is reassuring. One who cannot name a failure, or blames others, is a risk.

How to choose your failure

  • Real and yours. You made the call, or missed the warning sign. Not a team failure you watched.
  • With a visible cost. Time lost, money wasted, a target missed. Without a consequence there is no failure.
  • Manageable, not catastrophic. Avoid anything involving dishonesty or harm to others. You want a mistake of judgement, not of character.
  • Old enough to show change. You need time since then to have applied the lesson at least once.

A weak answer

I think my biggest failure is that I sometimes work too hard and take on too much, so I had to learn to delegate.

Why it falls short: it is not a failure; it is a disguised strength. There is no event, no consequence and no ownership, so it sounds rehearsed and avoids the question.

A strong answer

This example is illustrative; use your own.

In my first job I launched a customer survey without testing it on a small group first. Two of the questions were confusing, so about a third of the answers were unusable and we had to run it again, which delayed a pricing decision by a month. It was my call to skip the pilot to save a week. Since then I always test anything customer-facing with five or six people first. On my next project, that test caught a pricing error before launch.

Why it works: a real mistake with a real consequence, clear ownership ("it was my call"), a specific change in behaviour and evidence that the change worked. It takes about 40 seconds, leaving room for follow-ups.

A longer example, with numbers

If you have more time or the interviewer asks for detail, a fuller story might sound like this illustrative one:

I led a pilot of a new reporting dashboard. I assumed the team would use it because the metrics were useful, so I spent most of the first month building features and almost no time watching how managers actually made decisions. After two months only 40% of the intended users used it weekly, against a goal of 70%. I interviewed six colleagues and found the dashboard duplicated a morning report they already relied on, and left out the one breakdown they needed. I cut it back, added that breakdown and introduced it through existing team meetings. In the next pilot, weekly use reached 72%. The mistake was treating a finished product as proof it was useful.

Notice how the time is spent: two sentences on what went wrong, one on the consequence, and the rest on diagnosis, the fix and the lesson. The lesson is credible because the behaviour changed: the candidate now tests how people work before building more.

Handle the follow-up honestly

A good interviewer may ask, "Why didn't you catch it earlier?" State your responsibility plainly, including any warning signs you missed. If things turned out well in the end, still acknowledge what the original mistake cost. Do not drift into "but really it was the timeline" or "my manager approved it". The moment you shift blame, the story stops working.

Common mistakes

  • The disguised strength. "I care too much", "I'm a perfectionist". Interviewers have heard it hundreds of times.
  • Blaming others. Even if others contributed, focus on your part.
  • A trivial failure. Missing a bus is not a failure that teaches anything about work.
  • A vague lesson. "I learned to work harder" is not a repeatable change. Name the specific habit.
  • Dwelling on the failure. Keep the bad news short and spend most of your time on the response.

Try it now

1. What is wrong with this lesson? "I learned that communication is really important."

Show the answer

It is true of everything, so it says nothing. Replace it with a specific habit: "I now send a one-paragraph summary of decisions after every client call, so nobody leaves with a different understanding."

2. Your failure story ends with "but in the end the project succeeded anyway". Should you keep that line?

Show the answer

Only if you still acknowledge the cost of your mistake, such as a delay or extra work. Otherwise it sounds as if the failure did not matter, which undermines the point of the story.

3. Write your failure in four parts: what happened, your part in it, the consequence, and what you now do differently, with one example of using it.

Show the answer

Check the balance: the last part should be at least half the answer. Check ownership: does your second sentence contain "I"? And check the evidence: can you name a specific later occasion when the new habit helped?

Where to practise next

The failure question is close to the weakness question, so make sure you use different stories. Add your failure to your story bank using the fit interview guide, and see the most common fit questions for what else to prepare.
